grammar.title: Frase
grammar.rule: Eu falo; você fala. Eu preparo café; você prepara uma cadeira.
grammar.note_en:
Eu means “I,” the current speaker. Você means “you,” one person being addressed. When Ana says Eu trabalho aqui (“I work here”), eu refers to Ana. If Bia says the same sentence, it refers to Bia. In Você trabalha aqui também, Bia (“You work here too, Bia”), the named addressee identifies você as Bia. Meu/minha already changed their reference with the speaker; eu does too. Você refers to the listener but takes the same verb form as a singular named person: Ana fala means “Ana speaks”; você fala means “you speak.” Do not copy English you into a plural Portuguese verb form.

For the regular -ar verbs encountered here, the eu form ends in -o and the você form in -a: falo/fala (“I speak / you speak”), trabalho/trabalha (“I work / you work”), ajudo/ajuda (“I help / you help”), moro/mora (“I live / you live”), gosto/gosta (“I like / you like”), preciso/precisa (“I need / you need”), preparo/prepara (“I prepare / you prepare”), compro/compra (“I buy / you buy”), espero/espera (“I wait / you wait”), escuto/escuta (“I listen / you listen”), começo/começa (“I begin / you begin”), termino/termina (“I finish / you finish”). These are actual story forms, not an instruction to produce a full paradigm. In começar, the first-person spelling is começo with ç before o, while começa has ç before a as well. Do not omit the cedilla. These regular forms are not a rule for every verb ending in o or a.

The subject can be omitted when the context identifies it. Ana answers Preciso (“I need [them]”) after Rosa asks Você precisa de livros? (“Do you need books?”). Bia says Moro perto (“I live nearby”), and Rosa replies Gosto (“I like [it]”) to the coffee question. Omission does not change the verb form or speaker. Sou Rosa means “I am Rosa,” identifying the caller; não tenho café means “I do not have coffee.” Sou and tenho are the actual singular forms of ser and ter used here, not regular -ar examples. Other persons of those verbs are not introduced by this table.

Gostar takes de before the thing liked: Eu gosto de café means “I like coffee”; Você gosta de livros? means “Do you like books?” Precisar takes de before the thing needed here: Eu preciso de uma cadeira means “I need a chair”; Você precisa de café means “You need coffee.” These are noun complements, not a new licence for untaught infinitive constructions. Escutar directly takes its object: Eu escuto você means “I listen to you,” without inserting a Portuguese preposition to match English to. Falar com names the person spoken with: Eu falo com Bia means “I speak with Bia.” Esperar directly names the person waited for: Eu espero Bia means “I wait for Bia.” Morar names residence: Moro perto do café means “I live near the café”; it does not mean simply standing in the café now.

Café has two context-dependent meanings here: the place, already known, and the drink, newly taught. Rosa prepara café means “Rosa prepares coffee”; Ana trabalha no café means “Ana works at the café.” The cup, black drink and preparation support the new meaning. The word alone does not tell Ana whether she should buy supplies or prepare the drink: Eu compro café? (“Do I buy coffee?”) and Eu preparo café? (“Do I prepare coffee?”) name different actions. The complete written division resolves that uncertainty: Ana fala com as pessoas (“Ana speaks with the people”); Rosa prepara café (“Rosa prepares coffee”); Bia ajuda Ana (“Bia helps Ana”); Paulo leva os livros (“Paulo carries the books”). Trabalhar and ajudar do not erase these different jobs.

The five chairs are the same five already counted. The new list adds a female friend of Rosa, explicitly not Bia, and a male friend of Paulo to the four named people. These friends are entries for the proposed night, not newly arrived people in the café. Moving the window chair changes its location, not the total. The unpaired friend in the final comparison establishes a shortage without introducing an untaught number word or claiming that the evening has already taken place.

Verb names such as falar and trabalhar are dictionary forms, called infinitives. They label an action rather than identify its speaker. For the regular -ar pattern here, remove -ar and add -o for eu or -a for você: falar → fal- → falo/fala (“speak → I speak/you speak”). These labels explain the encountered forms; no unseen infinitive construction is an exercise answer. Preparing a chair here means making it ready: Ana removes her bag, while Bia brings the window chair to the table. Beginning and finishing refer to that same five-chair task. The final de phrases assign the chairs for the planned night; they do not transfer legal ownership of the café’s furniture.
